title: Chimichurri
summary: Bright, garlicky, and built for anything that came off the fire.
story: Chimichurri is Argentina's answer to steak sauce, and it embarrasses the bottled stuff. Parsley, oregano, garlic, and red pepper flakes swimming in good olive oil — chop it by hand, let it sit, and spoon it over everything.

items: 1/4 cup fresh oregano leaves, finely chopped (or 2 Tbsp dried)

steps.title: Chop
steps.body: Chop everything by hand — don't food-process it into baby food. You want texture.

steps.title: Mix & rest
steps.body: Stir it all together in a bowl. Let it sit at room temperature for at least 30 minutes so the flavors marry.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Spoon it over sliced brisket, tri-tip, chicken, or anything grilled.

proTips: Keeps a week in the fridge. The oil will solidify — let it come back to room temp before serving.
More heat? Double the red pepper flakes. Less? Leave them out entirely.

title: Smoked Spam Burnt Ends
summary: Cubed, rubbed sweet with Smoke & Ember rub, smoked, and glazed with Smoke & Ember sauce. Poor man's burnt ends that eat like candy.
story: Don't sleep on Spam. Cube it, hit it with Smoke & Ember Sweet Rub, and smoke it until the edges caramelize — then drown it in Smoke & Ember BBQ Sauce glaze and give it one more ride. These eat like meat candy.

items: 2 cans (12 oz each) Spam, cut into 1-inch cubes

steps.title: Cube & rub
steps.body: Cut the Spam into 1-inch cubes. Toss them in mustard as a binder if you want — helps the rub stick. Coat every cube generously with Smoke & Ember Sweet Rub.

steps.title: First smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 250°F over hickory or apple for 2 hours, until the edges start to crisp and caramelize.

steps.title: Glaze & pan
steps.body: Toss the cubes in the Smoke & Ember BBQ Sauce glaze. Put them in a foil pan, cover with foil, and back on the smoker for 1 more hour.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Uncover and give them 15 more minutes so the glaze gets sticky and tacky.

proTips: Don't skip the second smoke in the pan — that's where they go from good to candy.
Two cans sounds like a lot until they're gone in ten minutes.

title: Smoked Frog Legs
summary: Brined, smoked, then flash-fried. Crispy outside, tender inside — tastes like the bayou.
story: Frog legs done right are something special. A buttermilk brine pulls out any gaminess, a kiss of pecan smoke lays down flavor, and a hot fry finishes them crispy. If you've never had them — they taste like a cross between chicken and fish.

items: 2 lbs frog legs (hind legs only), thawed if frozen

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Soak the frog legs in the buttermilk, hot sauce, and salt for at least 2 hours — overnight is better.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pat them dry (don't rinse). Smoke at 225°F over pecan or oak for 45 minutes. You're laying down smoke, not cooking them through.

steps.title: Dredge
steps.body: Heat oil to 350°F in a cast iron skillet or fryer. Dredge the smoked legs in the flour-cornmeal mix, pressing it on good.

steps.title: Fry
steps.body: Fry 3-4 minutes per side until golden brown and crispy. Drain on a rack, not paper towels — keeps them crispy.

proTips: Don't overcook them. Frog legs go from perfect to rubber in about a minute.
Want to kick it up? Add a little cayenne pepper to the dredge.
Remoulade or comeback sauce for dipping. Hot sauce works too.

title: Pacific Island Pork Butt
summary: Pacific Island flair — smoked pork butt braised in coconut milk, soy, vinegar, and hot peppers until it falls apart.
story: Inspired by Manny, my buddy in Saipan, who told me they cook pork butt with coconut milk over there. I gave it the Smoke & Ember treatment — smoke it first for bark and flavor, then braise it island-style until it shreds. Serve it over rice and don't be shy with the sauce.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Season the pork butt with salt and pepper. Smoke at 250°F for 4 hours — building bark and smoke flavor, not finishing it.

steps.title: Braise
steps.body: Put the butt in a large pot or Dutch oven. Add everything else around it.

steps.title: Low & slow
steps.body: Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook low 3-4 hours, turning the butt once halfway. Done when it shreds with a fork.

steps.title: Soak
steps.body: Pull the pork apart in the pot and let it soak up the sauce for 15 minutes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve over white rice with plenty of the braising liquid spooned on top.

proTips: The vinegar and soy are the backbone — don't skip either one.
Coconut milk goes in for richness.
This makes a lot of sauce. That's the point — it's for the rice.

title: Pacific Island Parrotfish in Coconut Milk
summary: Pacific Island flair — parrotfish (uhu) simmered in coconut milk with onion, tomato, and a little heat.
story: Inspired by Manny, my buddy in Saipan, who gave this one the thumbs up. Island-style parrotfish simmered gentle in coconut milk — the kind of dish that makes you wish you lived closer to the water.

items: 2 lbs parrotfish fillets (uhu), cut into chunks

steps.title: Prep fish
steps.body: Season the fish with salt and pepper. Lightly dust with flour.

steps.title: Brown
steps.body: Brown the fish quickly in hot oil, just a minute per side. Pull it out.

steps.title: Sauce
steps.body: In the same pot, soften the onion and garlic. Add the coconut milk, tomatoes, lemon juice, salt, and hot pepper.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Bring to a gentle simmer — don't boil it hard or the coconut milk gets lumpy. Lay the fish back in and simmer 10-12 minutes until it flakes.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve over rice with the sauce spooned over everything.

proTips: Don't walk away from coconut milk on high heat. Low and gentle wins.
Any firm white fish works if you can't get parrotfish — but the real thing is worth it.

title: Kentucky Fried Chicken (Copycat)
summary: The 11 herbs and spices, as close as anyone's ever gotten. Deep fry it or grill it — cook's choice.
story: This is the Colonel's recipe as close as it gets outside the vault. White pepper is the secret — that's the back-of-the-throat heat you remember. Deep fry it classic style, or do the grill vortex method with no oil bath.

items: 1 whole chicken (3-4 lbs), cut into 8 pieces
2 cups flour mixed with all the spices above

steps.title: Soak
steps.body: Soak the chicken in buttermilk and beaten egg for 30 minutes.

steps.title: Dredge
steps.body: Mix the flour and all 11 spices. Pull each piece from the buttermilk, dredge in the seasoned flour, and rest on a wire rack for 15 minutes to set the crust.

steps.title: Cook — pick your method
steps.body: DEEP FRY: Fry at 350°F in shortening for 12-18 minutes depending on the piece. GRILL: Pile coals in a vortex (or center), arrange chicken around the edge, lid on at 400-450°F for 30-40 minutes, flipping once. No oil needed.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Drain on a wire rack. 165°F inside. Don't cut into it right away — let it rest 5 minutes.

proTips: The real KFC is pressure-fried — you can't do that at home safely, but this gets you 95% of the way on flavor.
Don't skip the rest before cooking. That's what keeps the breading on.
Shortening over oil for frying — that's the move.

title: Lee's Famous Recipe Chicken (Copycat)
summary: Lighter and crispier than KFC — the Colonel's nephew's recipe, big in Kentucky.
story: Lee's was started by Lee Cummings — Colonel Sanders' own nephew. It's huge in Kentucky but most folks outside the state never heard of it. Lighter, crispier crust than KFC thanks to self-rising flour. The underdog Kentucky chicken, and their loss is your gain.

items: 1 whole chicken (3-4 lbs), cut into 8 pieces
3 cups self-rising flour mixed with 1/4 cup of the spice blend

steps.title: Brine
steps.body: Brine the chicken in buttermilk and salt for at least 4 hours — overnight is better.

steps.title: Dredge
steps.body: Mix the self-rising flour with the spice blend. Pull each piece from the brine, dredge in the seasoned flour, pressing it on. Rest 10 minutes.

steps.title: Fry
steps.body: Fry at 325°F for 12-15 minutes until deep golden and crispy. 165°F inside.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Drain on a wire rack and rest 10 minutes before serving.

proTips: Self-rising flour is non-negotiable — that's what makes the crust light and puffy.
Fry a touch lower than KFC (325°F) so the lighter crust doesn't burn before the chicken cooks through.

title: Cinnamon-Spiced Pork Belly Rolls
summary: Pork belly strips rolled tight with cinnamon-forward Ember rub, smoked, and finished with Ember finishing glaze.
story: Not a dessert — a savory pork belly roll with warm cinnamon spice running through it. Rolled tight, smoked until probe-tender, and lacquered with Ember Finishing Glaze. Serve them on skewers and watch them disappear.

steps.title: Slice
steps.body: Slice the pork belly into long strips, about 1 1/2 inches wide.

steps.title: Rub
steps.body: Coat every strip generously with the cinnamon-esque rub — get it in all the cracks.

steps.title: Roll
steps.body: Roll each strip up tight and tie with twine or skewer through to hold the shape.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 275°F until 200-205°F internal, about 2-3 hours. You want them probe-tender like burnt ends.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Brush with warmed Ember Finishing Glaze during the last 30 minutes. Don't be shy — coat them completely.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Rest 15 minutes. Serve on the skewers with extra glaze for dipping.

proTips: The cinnamon reads as warm spice, not dessert. The cayenne and ginger keep it honest.
Tie them tight or they'll unroll on you.
Cut the twine off before serving unless you want someone flossing with it.

title: Ember Pumpkin Spice Pork Rub
summary: A fall-seasonal Ember rub — warm pumpkin spice built for pork butt, ribs, belly, and loin.
story: Pork and warm spice are old friends — clove-studded ham, apple-cinnamon pork loin. This just puts a name on it. Brown sugar and pumpkin pie spices with enough cayenne to keep the sweet honest. A Halloween-season Ember rub: put it on everything in October and retire it with honor.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Stir everything together until evenly combined.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: Coat pork butt, ribs, belly, or loin generously. Smoke or grill as usual.

steps.title: Store
steps.body: Keeps in a sealed jar for 6 months — but you won't need it that long in October.

proTips: Don't go heavy-handed past 1/2 tsp on the cloves or it'll taste like a ham from 1974.
Killer on a smoked pork loin with an apple glaze.
Or use your favorite rub — it's not set in stone.

title: Ember Pumpkin Spice BBQ Sauce
summary: A fall BBQ sauce — warm pumpkin spice over a tangy apple-cider base. Built for the pumpkin spice rub.
story: Every great rub deserves a sauce that speaks its language. Apple butter gives this one body and fall-orchard flavor, pumpkin pie spices bring the warmth, and a splash of bourbon keeps it grown-up. Brush it on in the last 15 minutes and let the sugars caramelize. The full October treatment, start to finish.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Everything in a saucepan. Stir it smooth.

steps.title: Simmer
steps.body: Simmer low for 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until it thickens enough to coat a spoon.

steps.title: Taste
steps.body: Want more tang? Another splash of vinegar. More warm? Another pinch of cinnamon.

steps.title: Jar
steps.body: Cool and jar it. Keeps 3 weeks in the fridge.

proTips: Brush it on ribs or pork loin in the last 15 minutes so the sugars caramelize instead of burn.
Pair it with the Ember Pumpkin Spice Pork Rub for the full October treatment.
Or use your favorite sauce — it's not set in stone.

title: Pumpkin-Spiced Grilled Sweet Potatoes
summary: Sweet potato cubes tossed in Ember pumpkin spice rub, grilled until caramelized and crispy-edged.
story: The side dish that eats like dessert but isn't. Sweet potatoes love warm spice the way pork does — toss them in the Ember pumpkin spice rub with butter and brown sugar, hit them with high heat, and let the edges go crispy and caramelized. They go scary-good next to anything with the pumpkin spice sauce on it.

items: 3 lbs sweet potatoes, peeled and cut into 1-inch cubes
3 Tbsp Ember Pumpkin Spice Pork Rub

steps.title: Toss
steps.body: Toss the cubes with melted butter until every piece is coated.

steps.title: Season
steps.body: Sprinkle the rub, brown sugar, and salt over them. Toss again — get it even.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over medium-high heat (about 400°F) in a grill basket or on a sheet pan, 20-25 minutes, turning once. You want crispy caramelized edges. No grill? Roast at 425°F in the oven, same time.

proTips: Cut them even or the small ones burn while the big ones stay hard. One inch, no heroes.
The brown sugar's what gives you those crispy edges — don't skip it.
Or use your favorite rub — it's not set in stone.

title: Venison Pineapple Bratwurst
summary: Sweet pineapple meets savory bratwurst spices in a venison sausage. The Amish know what they're doing.
story: Every year I get a deer, I take it to the Amish and have them turn some of it into pineapple bratwurst. Sweet, savory, juicy — it's the sausage I look forward to all year. This is my version of it: venison and pork butt, crushed pineapple, and classic bratwurst spices, stuffed into hog casings and smoked low.

items: 1 can (20 oz) crushed pineapple, drained well

steps.title: Grind
steps.body: Grind the venison and pork butt together through a coarse plate. Keep everything cold — meat, grinder, all of it.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix in the drained pineapple and all the spices. Add the ice water and mix until it gets sticky and binds together.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Stuff into hog casings, twist into 6-inch links. Don't overstuff or they'll burst.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Smoke at 180-200°F until they hit 155°F internal, about 2-3 hours. Or grill them over medium heat.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes before cutting in.

proTips: Drain that pineapple GOOD. Squeeze it in a towel if you have to. Too much juice and the sausage won't bind.
The pork butt's non-negotiable — straight venison bratwurst comes out dry as a bone.
Or use your favorite sausage seasoning — it's not set in stone.
